questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Converting degrees to radians
questions.learningObjective: convert an angle given in degrees into an exact radian measure
questions.practice: working with converting degrees to radians in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: An angle measures 150 degrees. Which expression in terms of pi gives the same angle in radians?

options.misconception: scales by pi over 90 instead of pi over 180, which is 135 degrees
doubles the degree value instead of scaling it, giving 300 degrees
adds a half turn of 180 degrees before converting, giving 210 degrees

questions.explanation: Radians and degrees measure the same angle on different scales, so the conversion is a ratio of the two full-turn sizes: multiply by pi over 180. That gives 150 times pi over 180, which reduces because 150 and 180 share a factor of 30, leaving 5 times pi over 6. Reading the distractors back in degrees confirms the errors: 3 times pi over 4 is 135 degrees, which is what you get from using 90 instead of 180 as the half-turn divisor; 5 times pi over 3 is 300 degrees, the result of doubling the angle instead of scaling it; and 7 times pi over 6 is 210 degrees, which only appears if a half turn is added first.
questions.hint: There are pi radians in 180 degrees, so scale 150 by pi over 180 and simplify.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Converting radians to degrees
questions.learningObjective: convert an exact radian measure into degrees
questions.practice: working with converting radians to degrees in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: The angle 7*pi/6 radians is coterminal with a positive angle. What is that angle in degrees?
questions.explanation: The reverse conversion multiplies by 180 over pi, so 7 times pi over 6 becomes 7 times 180 over 6, and 180 over 6 is 30, leaving 7 times 30, which is 210. A second route agrees: 210 degrees is a little more than a half turn of 180, and since 7 times pi over 6 is pi over 6 past pi, it must sit 30 degrees beyond 180 in the second quadrant region of the full turn. Both give 210.
questions.hint: Multiply 7*pi/6 by 180/pi; the pi cancels and only the numbers remain.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Arc length from a central angle in radians
questions.learningObjective: compute an arc length from a radius and a radian central angle
questions.practice: working with arc length from a central angle in radians in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: A circle has radius 9. A central angle of 2*pi/3 radians cuts off an arc. What is the length of that arc?
questions.explanation: On a circle of radius r a central angle of theta radians sweeps an arc of length r times theta, so here the arc is 9 times 2 times pi over 3, which is 6 times pi. The circumference route confirms it: an angle of 2*pi over 3 is exactly two thirds of the full turn 2*pi, and two thirds of the circumference 2 times pi times 9 is 6 times pi as well. The two independent computations give the same value, about 18.8496.
questions.hint: Multiply the radius by the radian measure; cross-check by taking the stated fraction of the circumference.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Sector area from a central angle in radians
questions.learningObjective: compute a sector area from a radius and a radian central angle
questions.practice: working with sector area from a central angle in radians in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: A sector of a circle of radius 6 is cut off by a central angle of 5*pi/6 radians. What is the area of the sector?
questions.explanation: The sector area is one half of r squared times theta, so here it is one half of 36 times 5 times pi over 6, and 36 over 6 is 6, leaving one half of 6 times 5 times pi, which is 15 times pi. The fraction-of-a-circle route gives the same result independently: the sector is 5 over 12 of the full circle, and 5 over 12 of pi times 6 squared is 5 over 12 of 36 times pi, again 15 times pi. Both computations agree on about 47.1239.
questions.hint: Use one half of r squared times theta, then confirm by taking the same fraction of the full circle.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Reading coordinates on the unit circle
questions.learningObjective: read the cosine and sine coordinates of a point on the unit circle
questions.practice: working with reading coordinates on the unit circle in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: On the unit circle, a point at angle 5*pi/6 is placed in the second quadrant. What are the coordinates of that point?

options.misconception: keeps the cosine positive in the second quadrant, giving the point at pi/6
swaps cosine and sine, giving the point at 2*pi/3
also negates the sine, placing the point in the third quadrant at 7*pi/6

questions.explanation: On the unit circle the first coordinate is the cosine and the second is the sine. The reference angle for 5 times pi over 6 is pi over 6, where the coordinates are cos of pi over 6 equals sqrt(3) over 2 and sin of pi over 6 equals 1 over 2. Because 5 times pi over 6 lies in the second quadrant the cosine is negative while the sine stays positive, giving the point (-sqrt(3)/2, 1/2). The Pythagorean identity checks it: 3 over 4 plus 1 over 4 is 1, so the point really is on the circle of radius 1.
questions.hint: The second quadrant keeps sine positive and flips the cosine; the reference angle is pi/6.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Trigonometric ratios in a right triangle
questions.learningObjective: read a trigonometric ratio from the sides of a right triangle
questions.practice: working with trigonometric ratios in a right triangle in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: In a right triangle, the side opposite the angle A measures 12 units and the hypotenuse measures 20 units. What is the sine of angle A?
questions.explanation: The sine of an angle in a right triangle is the opposite side over the hypotenuse, so it is 12 over 20, which is 0.6. The Pythagorean identity gives the same answer by a different route: with sine at 0.6 the cosine must be the square root of 1 minus 0.36, which is the square root of 0.64, that is 0.8, and 20 times 0.8 is 16, so the other leg is 16 and the sides 12, 16, 20 satisfy the identity 144 plus 256 equals 400. Both routes agree the sine is 0.6.
questions.hint: Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, so divide 12 by 20.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The 30-60-90 triangle ratios
questions.learningObjective: use the fixed side ratios of a 30-60-90 triangle
questions.practice: working with the 30-60-90 triangle ratios in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: A 30-60-90 right triangle has a hypotenuse of length 14. What is the exact length of the side opposite the 60 degree angle?
questions.explanation: The sides of a 30-60-90 triangle stand in the ratio 1 to sqrt(3) to 2, with the hypotenuse twice the short leg. The side opposite the 60 degree angle is the long leg, so it is sqrt(3) over 2 times the hypotenuse, that is sqrt(3) over 2 times 14, which is 7 times sqrt(3), about 12.1244. Building the triangle from the other end gives the same number: the short leg opposite 30 degrees is 7, and then the Pythagorean identity makes the long leg the square root of 14 squared minus 7 squared, that is the square root of 147, again 7 times sqrt(3).
questions.hint: The long leg is sqrt(3)/2 times the hypotenuse; confirm by Pythagoras from the short leg.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The 45-45-90 triangle ratios
questions.learningObjective: use the fixed side ratios of a 45-45-90 triangle
questions.practice: working with the 45-45-90 triangle ratios in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: A 45-45-90 right triangle has a hypotenuse of length 9*sqrt(2). What is the length of each leg?
questions.explanation: In a 45-45-90 triangle the legs are equal and the hypotenuse is that common leg times sqrt(2). So each leg is the hypotenuse divided by sqrt(2), which is 9 times sqrt(2) over sqrt(2), and rationalising by multiplying top and bottom by sqrt(2) turns 9 times sqrt(2) over sqrt(2) into 9 times 2 over 2, that is 9. The Pythagorean identity confirms it directly: two legs of 9 give 81 plus 81, which is 162, and the square root of 162 is 9 times sqrt(2), exactly the hypotenuse given.
questions.hint: Each leg is the hypotenuse divided by sqrt(2); confirm with the Pythagorean identity.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The sign of a trig function in each quadrant
questions.learningObjective: determine the signs of sine, cosine and tangent in a given quadrant
questions.practice: working with the sign of a trig function in each quadrant in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: An angle lies in the third quadrant, so its reference angle is less than pi/2. Which set of signs holds for its sine, cosine and tangent?

options.text: sine positive, cosine positive, tangent positive
options.misconception: assumes the pattern of the first quadrant, where the angle is still in the upper right

options.text: sine negative, cosine positive, tangent negative
options.misconception: uses the fourth quadrant pattern, where only the cosine is positive

options.text: sine negative, cosine negative, tangent positive
sine positive, cosine negative, tangent negative
options.misconception: uses the second quadrant pattern, where the sine is still positive

questions.explanation: The sign pattern follows from the unit circle itself. In the third quadrant the point has moved past 180 degrees, so both coordinates are negative: the cosine, which is the horizontal coordinate, is negative, and the sine, which is the vertical coordinate, is negative. The tangent is the sine divided by the cosine, and a negative divided by a negative is positive, so the tangent is positive. Checking at 210 degrees, where sine is -1 over 2 and cosine is -sqrt(3) over 2, the quotient is 1 over sqrt(3), which is positive, confirming the pattern.
questions.hint: Both coordinates are negative past 180 degrees, and a quotient of two negatives is positive.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Coterminal angles
questions.learningObjective: reduce an angle to an equivalent angle in a stated interval
questions.practice: working with coterminal angles in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: The angle -7*pi/6 is coterminal with an angle that lies between 0 and 2*pi. What is that angle, in degrees?
questions.explanation: Coterminal angles differ by whole turns, so add multiples of 2*pi until the value is positive. Starting from -7 times pi over 6, adding 2 times pi, which is 12 times pi over 6, gives 5 times pi over 6, and that is already between 0 and 2 times pi. Converting it to degrees, 5 times pi over 6 times 180 over pi is 150. Working in degrees from the start gives the same answer: -7 times pi over 6 is -210 degrees, and adding the 360 degrees of one full turn once gives 150.
questions.hint: Add full turns until the angle is positive, then convert to degrees.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Reference angle of a given angle
questions.learningObjective: find the reference angle of an angle given in degrees
questions.practice: working with reference angle of a given angle in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: What is the reference angle of an angle of 250 degrees?
questions.explanation: A reference angle is the acute angle on the unit circle that shares a side with the given angle, and in the third quadrant it is the angle minus 180, so 250 minus 180 is 70. Measuring the other way round agrees: the angle is 360 minus 250, that is 110, short of the full turn, and the remaining part of the second quadrant is 180 minus 110, again 70. Both routes land on the same acute angle, which is what makes the reference angle useful for evaluating the trigonometric functions of 250 degrees.
questions.hint: In the third quadrant the reference angle is the angle minus 180.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Evaluating sine in the second quadrant
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the sine of an angle in the second quadrant exactly
questions.practice: working with evaluating sine in the second quadrant in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: What is the exact value of the sine of 2*pi/3 radians?
questions.explanation: The angle 2 times pi over 3 sits in the second quadrant with reference angle pi over 3, so its sine is the sine of pi over 3, which is sqrt(3) over 2. The Pythagorean identity confirms it independently: the cosine of 2 times pi over 3 is -1 over 2, so the sine must be the square root of 1 minus 1 over 4, which is the square root of 3 over 4, that is sqrt(3) over 2, and the positive root is taken because the sine is positive in the second quadrant. In decimal form that is about 0.866025.
questions.hint: The sine equals the sine of the reference angle pi/3, so it is sqrt(3)/2.

questions.topic: Evaluating cosine in the third quadrant
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the cosine of an angle in the third quadrant exactly
questions.practice: working with evaluating cosine in the third quadrant in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: What is the exact value of the cosine of 7*pi/6 radians?
questions.explanation: The angle 7 times pi over 6 lies in the third quadrant with reference angle pi over 6, and there the cosine is negative. Since the cosine of pi over 6 is sqrt(3) over 2, the cosine of 7 times pi over 6 is minus sqrt(3) over 2. Reading it off the unit circle gives the same sign, because a point below and to the left of the origin has a negative horizontal coordinate. As a check the sine there is -1 over 2, and 3 over 4 plus 1 over 4 is 1, so the point is on the circle as it should be.
questions.hint: Use the reference angle pi/6 for the size and the third quadrant for the negative sign.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Evaluating tangent in the fourth quadrant
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the tangent of an angle in the fourth quadrant exactly
questions.practice: working with evaluating tangent in the fourth quadrant in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: What is the exact value of the tangent of 11*pi/6 radians?
questions.explanation: The angle 11 times pi over 6 lies in the fourth quadrant, whose reference angle is pi over 6. There the tangent is the sine divided by the cosine, so it is 1 over 2 divided by sqrt(3) over 2, which is 1 over sqrt(3), and rationalising gives sqrt(3) over 3. The fourth quadrant makes the tangent negative because the sine is negative while the cosine is positive, so the exact value is minus sqrt(3) over 3, about -0.577350. Using the reference angle for the size and the quadrant for the sign is the reliable rule here.
questions.hint: The tangent equals the sine over the cosine, which is 1 over 2 divided by sqrt(3) over 2; the fourth quadrant makes the result negative.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The reciprocal identity for secant
questions.learningObjective: state the reciprocal identity that defines the secant in terms of cosine
questions.practice: working with the reciprocal identity for secant in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: Which equation correctly states the reciprocal identity involving the secant of an angle?

options.text: sec of theta equals cos of theta divided by sin of theta
options.misconception: states the quotient identity for tangent, which is sin over cos not cos over sin

options.text: sec of theta equals 1 over cos of theta
sec of theta equals 1 minus cos of theta
options.misconception: subtracts instead of inverting, which destroys the reciprocal structure entirely

options.text: sec of theta equals sin of theta divided by cos of theta
options.misconception: repeats the tangent quotient identity under the wrong name

questions.explanation: The three reciprocal identities pair each of the six trigonometric functions with the reciprocal of the other one: secant is the reciprocal of cosine, cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, and cotangent is the reciprocal of tangent. So secant of theta equals 1 over cosine of theta, valid wherever the cosine is not zero. The restriction is not decoration: at 90 degrees the cosine vanishes, so the secant is undefined there, and the secant graph has a vertical asymptote exactly on those angles.
questions.hint: Secant is defined as one over cosine, wherever the cosine is not zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The reciprocal identity for cosecant
questions.learningObjective: state the reciprocal identity that defines the cosecant in terms of sine
questions.practice: working with the reciprocal identity for cosecant in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: Which equation correctly states the reciprocal identity involving the cosecant of an angle?

options.text: csc of theta equals sin of theta divided by cos of theta
options.misconception: confuses the cosecant with the tangent quotient, which uses sine over cosine

options.text: csc of theta equals 1 minus sin of theta
options.misconception: subtracts rather than inverting, so no reciprocal relation remains

options.text: csc of theta equals cos of theta divided by sin of theta
options.misconception: reads the quotient backwards, which is cotangent rather than cosecant

options.text: csc of theta equals 1 over sin of theta

questions.explanation: The cosecant is defined as the reciprocal of the sine, so cosecant of theta equals 1 over sine of theta, for every angle whose sine is not zero. The zero angles are the multiples of 180 degrees, and the restriction matters because the cosecant graph blows up there. The other candidate equations all break the pattern of pairing a function with the reciprocal of its partner: cosecant has nothing to do with a quotient of sine and cosine, and a subtraction has no place in any of these identities.
questions.hint: Cosecant is one over sine, wherever the sine is not zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The quotient identity for tangent
questions.learningObjective: state the quotient identity that defines the tangent in terms of sine and cosine
questions.practice: working with the quotient identity for tangent in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: Which equation correctly expresses the tangent of an angle using the sine and the cosine?

options.text: tan of theta equals cos of theta divided by sin of theta
options.misconception: inverts the quotient, which produces the cotangent instead

options.text: tan of theta equals 1 over cos of theta
options.misconception: applies the secant reciprocal identity under the name tangent

options.text: tan of theta equals sin of theta divided by cos of theta
tan of theta equals 1 minus cos of theta
options.misconception: subtracts instead of dividing, abandoning every identity structure at once

questions.explanation: The tangent is a slope, a rise over a run, and on the unit circle the sine is the rise and the cosine is the run, so tangent of theta equals sine of theta divided by cosine of theta wherever the cosine is not zero. Inverting the quotient gives the cotangent rather than the tangent, and the reciprocal identity for the tangent pairs it with the cotangent, not with the cosine. The division by cosine is what makes the tangent undefined at 90 degrees and at every angle differing from it by a whole number of turns.
questions.hint: Tangent is rise over run, that is sine divided by cosine.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: The Pythagorean identity
questions.learningObjective: state the Pythagorean identity linking sine and cosine
questions.practice: working with the pythagorean identity in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: Which equation is the Pythagorean identity for an arbitrary angle?

options.text: sin squared of theta plus cos squared of theta equals 1
sin of theta plus cos of theta equals 1
options.misconception: drops the squares, which only holds at the special angles where an angle is complementary to itself

options.text: sin of theta divided by cos of theta equals 1
options.misconception: confuses the Pythagorean identity with the quotient identity for tangent

options.text: sin squared of theta minus cos squared of theta equals 1
options.misconception: changes a plus into a minus, which is a different identity altogether

questions.explanation: On the unit circle the horizontal and vertical coordinates are the cosine and the sine, and those coordinates satisfy the Pythagorean identity because the radius is 1. So for every angle, sine squared plus cosine squared is 1. The identity needs no restriction on the angle, unlike the quotient and reciprocal identities, because no division occurs. Its practical use is solving for one function when the other is known, taking care to choose the sign that matches the quadrant the angle lies in.
questions.hint: It comes straight from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit circle.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Isolating one function with the Pythagorean identity
questions.learningObjective: simplify a quotient using the Pythagorean identity
questions.practice: working with isolating one function with the pythagorean identity in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: Which expression is equal to the fraction with numerator 1 minus cos squared of theta and denominator sin of theta, for every theta where the fraction is defined?

options.text: the fraction with numerator sin of theta and denominator cos of theta
options.misconception: cancels down to the tangent quotient instead of stopping at a single sine

options.text: sin of theta alone, with the squared factor cancelled from the fraction
the fraction with numerator 1 and denominator sin squared of theta
options.misconception: inverts the whole fraction instead of using the identity on the numerator

options.text: cos of theta divided by sin of theta
options.misconception: arrives at the cotangent, which is the reciprocal of the correct simplified form

questions.explanation: The numerator 1 minus cosine squared is exactly the sine squared by the Pythagorean identity, so the fraction becomes sine squared over sine, and cancelling one factor of sine leaves a single sine. Two conditions come with this. The fraction is undefined where the sine vanishes, and it is only then undefined: the squared cosine is never 1 except at those same angles, so no zero of the numerator appears outside the zeros of the denominator. After the cancellation the result sine is defined everywhere, so the two expressions agree on their common domain even though only one is defined there.
questions.hint: Replace 1 minus cos squared by sin squared using the Pythagorean identity, then cancel one sine.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.topic: Cofunction identities linking sine to cosine
questions.learningObjective: state the cofunction identity relating the sine of an angle to the cosine of its complement
questions.practice: working with cofunction identities linking sine to cosine in an algebra and trigonometry context
questions.stem: Which equation states the cofunction identity that pairs the sine of an angle with the cosine of its complement?

options.text: sin of theta equals cos of the quantity 90 degrees minus theta
sin of theta equals cos of the quantity 180 degrees minus theta
options.misconception: uses the supplementary complement, which negates the value instead of preserving it

options.text: sin of theta equals cos of the quantity theta divided by 2
options.misconception: pairs the sine with a half angle rather than with its complement

options.text: sin of theta equals 1 minus cos of theta
options.misconception: invents a subtraction relation that no identity of the six functions provides

questions.explanation: A cofunction identity pairs complementary angles: the two acute angles of a right triangle. Since the complement of theta is 90 degrees minus theta, the sine of theta equals the cosine of 90 degrees minus theta, and the cosine of theta equals the sine of 90 degrees minus theta. On the unit circle this is visible as a swap of the two coordinates, reflecting across the line at 45 degrees. Testing at 30 degrees confirms the pair: sine of 30 degrees is 1 over 2 and cosine of 60 degrees is 1 over 2 as well.
questions.hint: Complementary angles swap their roles: sin of theta equals cos of 90 degrees minus theta.
